panels.rationale: Single-panel H&E (20x) skin biopsy from a real patient whose case is framed by the disease-focused title 'Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis Presented as Persistent Diaper Dermatitis' and the in-text histopathology of the persistent diaper-dermatitis lesion. The captioned 'ulcerated epidermis' maps to erosive diaper dermatitis (vocabulary: diaper_dermatitis_diaper_area_erosions, synonym Jacquet erosive dermatitis), supporting attribution to the configured disease diaper_dermatitis. Confidence is moderate because the section is histologic rather than a clinical photograph and the infiltrate is histiocytic (CD207/CD1a/S-100 context), i.e. the biopsy unmasked LCH rather than ordinary irritant dermatitis; no age, ethnicity, or Fitzpatrick-assessable skin surface is shown. [raw subtype: erosive diaper dermatitis]

panels.figure_caption: Histological section of the skin showing an ulcerated epidermis and inflammatory cell infiltrate in the dermis and epidermis (hematoxylin and eosin, 20x)
in_text_mentions: copic examination showed an ulcerated epidermis with fibrin, cellular debris, parakeratosis, irregular acanthosis, spongiosis, and hydropic degeneration of epidermal basal cells. In the dermis and epidermis, infiltration of abundant polygonal histiocytes with cytoplasmic vacuolation along with eosinophils, lymphocytes, and plasma cells was observed, being CD207, CD1a, and S-100 positive by immunohistochemistry (Figures 4, 5). Additionally, microabscesses were also noted. The histopathologic diagnosis was superficial perivascular dermatitis with a lichenoid pattern and histiocytic infiltration.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Clinical photograph of the diaper/genital distribution with marked erythema and scaling, directly matching diaper dermatitis vocabulary findings. B: Real patient photograph captioned as part of the initial presentation of diaper dermatitis; the disease-focused article title specifies disseminated diaper dermatitis with concomitant body rash, supporting attribution of this maculopapular body rash though it is not represented in the allowed findings vocabulary. C: Clinical photograph of the same patient showing the captioned trunk maculopapular rash on day 3; attribution to diaper dermatitis comes from the disease-focused case title describing disseminated diaper dermatitis with concomitant body rash, with moderate confidence because the body-rash finding is outside the allowed diaper-area vocabulary.
panels.attribution_text: Alapatt et al. Disseminated Diaper Dermatitis With Concomitant Body Rash: A Case Report.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.87273. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Initial presentation of diaper dermatitis (A) Genital area showing marked erythema, flaking, and scaling. (B) Maculopapular rash involving the face, hands, and chest, appearing on the third day. (C) Maculopapular rash on the trunk was also noted on the third day.
in_text_mentions: A six-month-old male with a history of redundant prepuce and phimosis presented to the office with a diaper rash that had begun five days earlier. The patient had experienced a similar-appearing diaper rash one month prior, which had resolved spontaneously without medical intervention. There were no preceding lesions, such as a herald patch, before the onset of the current diaper rash. According to the patient’s mother, a body rash developed on day 3 of the illness. An erythematous maculopapular rash was observed on the abdomen, chest, cheeks, arms, and hands (Figure 1).
